note: Ravina was walking with Mar bar Rav Ashi on Shabbat when a corner of Mar's garment, the one holding his ritual fringes, tore. In a second version of the story, Ravina told him on the spot, and Mar asked whether Ravina really expected him to throw his garment off in the street. He explained that human dignity overrides this rule, since the place they were walking was a karmelit, where carrying is forbidden only by rabbinic law.
why: The Gemara is asking why Mar bar Rav Ashi would have discarded the torn garment in public, given the teaching that human dignity overrides a prohibition. The answer is that dignity overrides only rabbinic prohibitions, and the second version fits the story to that rule.

terms.meaning: Tzitzit: the strings the Torah requires on the corners of a four-cornered garment. With one torn off, the garment no longer fulfils the commandment and may not be worn into the street on Shabbat.
An area that is neither a private home nor a true public thoroughfare, such as a field or a side street. Carrying there on Shabbat is forbidden only by rabbinic law.
A verse (Deuteronomy 17:11) telling Israel to follow the rulings of its Sages; the Gemara uses it as shorthand for laws made by the rabbis rather than written in the Torah.

flag: The first STORY segment begins mid-sentence, finishing an answer started in the previous segment; the actual event (the torn fringe) is told only in the BEFORE segments.

note: When a High Priest died and no successor had yet been appointed, his daily meal offering still had to be brought. At first it was paid for from public Temple funds, as the Torah requires. When the Sages saw the Temple treasury running low, they made the dead priest's heirs pay instead. When they saw the heirs neglecting it, they went back to paying from public funds.
why: A mishna lists public payment for this offering as one of seven rabbinic enactments, which seems to make it rabbinic rather than Torah law. Rabbi Abbahu answers that it is Torah law; the Sages changed it and then restored it, which is why it is listed.

people.name: Rabbi Abbahu
people.about: A Sage of the Land of Israel around 300 CE, based in Caesarea.

terms.meaning: The chief priest of the Temple in Jerusalem, who brought a special offering of flat cakes of flour and oil every day.
The Temple treasury room, holding funds collected from the whole people to pay for public offerings.
A rule enacted by the Sages, as distinct from one written in the Torah itself.
